25523: The setting is outside Israel: Uz is associated with Edom (Lam 4:21) or with Aram, and Job's friends come from Teman, Shuah and Naamah, regions linked with Edom and Arabia. Job acts as his own family priest, his wealth is measured in livestock, and he lives an extraordinarily long life, features that resemble the patriarchal age. The Hebrew is unusually difficult, with many rare words and some Aramaic influence. The heavenly figure called "the satan" (with the article) functions as an accuser in God's court, which many scholars distinguish from the later developed figure of Satan.
25524: Job has given language its proverbial "patience of Job" and "Job's comforters." The book is one of the most influential treatments of innocent suffering in world literature, shaping works from Gregory's *Moralia* to William Blake's engravings, Archibald MacLeish's *J.B.*, and Elie Wiesel's post-Holocaust reflections. In Islam, Ayyub is honored as a prophet known for patience.
25525: The *Testament of Job* expands the story, presenting Job as a king who destroyed an idol's temple and was therefore attacked by Satan, and giving his daughters heavenly sashes that enable them to speak in angelic tongues.
25526: Testament of Job (Jewish pseudepigraphon, c. 1st century BC to 1st century AD)
25527: The Septuagint adds an epilogue identifying Job with Jobab, king of Edom (Gen 36:33), and stating that he will rise again with those the Lord raises.
25529: Eloquent, passionate and poetic, swinging between bitter protest and reverent awe; speaks with the gravity of an elder who refuses easy answers and insists on honesty before God.
25534: Father who sought healing for his daughter
25535: Ruler of a synagogue (archisynagōgos), a lay leader who arranged the services
25537: Begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter
25538: When Jesus lands on the Galilean shore, Jairus falls at his feet and pleads for his twelve-year-old daughter, his only daughter in Luke's telling, who is near death.
25540: On the way, Jesus stops to speak with a woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years and touched his cloak. During the delay, word comes that the girl has died.
25542: Jesus tells Jairus, 'Do not fear, only believe.' Taking only Peter, James and John and the parents, he takes the girl's hand and says 'Talitha cumi' (Aramaic for 'little girl, arise'). She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them to give her something to eat.
25543: Jairus was a leader of a local synagogue in Galilee who came to Jesus when his twelve-year-old daughter was dying. Mark and Luke name him; Matthew tells a shorter version and calls him simply 'a ruler'. His story is wrapped around the healing of a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years, so the two stories are meant to be read together: both involve 'twelve years', both involve faith, and both involve a woman who is ritually unclean (by illness or death) being restored by Jesus' touch. The setting is by the Sea of Galilee, probably at or near Capernaum, though the text does not say so directly.
25544: Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 name him Jairus and call him a ruler of the synagogue. Luke 8:42 says the girl was his only daughter, about twelve years old. Matthew 9:18 says the ruler came saying his daughter had just died, a compressed form of the story. Mark 5:41 preserves Jesus' Aramaic words.
25546: The story shows that a respected religious official and an outcast woman come to Jesus on the same terms: need and trust.
25548: Many scholars see Mark's 'sandwich' technique here, where one story is placed inside another so each explains the other.
25549: A dignified man stripped of his dignity by fear for his child; speaks urgently, then in hushed wonder.
25557: Cries out to the Son of David and receives sight
25558: Sitting by the road outside Jericho, he shouts 'Son of David, have mercy on me' and refuses to be silenced. Jesus calls him, he throws off his cloak, asks to see again, is healed, and follows Jesus on the road toward Jerusalem.
25559: Bartimaeus was a blind beggar at Jericho healed by Jesus on his last journey to Jerusalem. Mark alone names him. Luke tells of one unnamed blind man (Luke 18:35-43), and Matthew of two (Matt 20:29-34). He is the only person Jesus heals in Mark who is said to follow him 'on the road' afterwards.
25560: Mark 10:46 says he was the son of Timaeus and sat by the roadside begging. He calls Jesus 'Son of David', a royal title for the Messiah (Mark 10:47). Jesus says his faith has made him well (Mark 10:52).
25562: Matthew's two men and Mark's one may be the same event: Mark and Luke focus on the better-known man, perhaps because Bartimaeus was later known to the church.
25564: Many scholars think Matthew doubled the figure (as he also does with the Gadarene demoniacs) and that the name in Mark points to an eyewitness known to Mark's first readers.
25565: Loud, stubborn and unembarrassed; he will not let a chance pass him by.
25567: Simon (from Hebrew Shimon, 'he has heard'); Cyrene was a city in North Africa (modern Libya)
25571: Coming in from the countryside, he is pressed into service by the Roman soldiers to carry Jesus' cross to the place of execution.
25572: Simon was a man from Cyrene, a North African city with a large Jewish community, who was in Jerusalem at Passover. Roman soldiers forced him to carry Jesus' cross. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus, which suggests Mark's readers knew those sons.
25573: Mark 15:21 calls him 'the father of Alexander and Rufus' and says he was coming in from the country. Matthew 27:32 and Luke 23:26 also tell the event; Luke says he carried it 'behind Jesus'.
25575: Some suggest the Rufus greeted in Romans 16:13 is his son, and some link him to 'Simeon called Niger' in Acts 13:1. Both are possible but unproven (speculative).
25577: Luke's phrase 'behind Jesus' echoes Jesus' call to take up the cross and follow (Luke 9:23), so Simon becomes a picture of discipleship.
25578: Some Gnostic writers taught that Simon was crucified in Jesus' place; the early church rejected this, and Irenaeus reports it as the teaching of Basilides.
25580: A plain-spoken traveller, startled at being dragged into a stranger's execution, later thoughtful about what he saw.
25582: 'Son of the father' (or son of a man named Abba)
25583: Jesus Barabbas (in some manuscripts of Matthew)
25587: Pilate offers to release a prisoner for the Passover. The crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, asks for Barabbas, and Jesus is handed over to be crucified.
25588: Barabbas was a prisoner held for taking part in a rebellion in Jerusalem in which a murder was committed. At Jesus' trial the crowd asked Pilate to free him instead of Jesus. All four Gospels tell the scene. Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him 'Jesus Barabbas', which would make the crowd's choice between two men named Jesus.
25589: Mark 15:7 says he was in prison with rebels who had committed murder in the uprising. Luke 23:19 says he was thrown into prison for insurrection and murder. John 18:40 calls him a lēstēs, a word for a bandit often used of armed rebels. Matthew 27:16 calls him a notorious prisoner.
25591: Many Christians see Barabbas as a picture of substitution: the guilty man goes free while the innocent one dies.
25593: No source outside the Gospels mentions a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover. Some historians doubt the custom; others point to known cases of Roman governors granting amnesties and argue a local practice is plausible.
25594: Hard and defiant, a man of the street fight, baffled at his sudden freedom.
25600: Household servant of the high priest
25601: Ear cut off and healed at the arrest
25602: When the crowd comes to arrest Jesus, Peter draws a sword and cuts off Malchus's right ear. Jesus tells Peter to put the sword away, and in Luke he touches the ear and heals it.
25603: Malchus was a servant of the high priest who came with the group that arrested Jesus in the garden. All four Gospels report that a disciple cut off a servant's ear, but only John names both the servant (Malchus) and the swordsman (Peter). Only Luke says Jesus healed the ear: the last healing miracle before the cross.
25604: John 18:10 gives his name and says it was the right ear. John 18:26 mentions a relative of Malchus who recognized Peter in the courtyard. Luke 22:51 says Jesus touched the ear and healed him. Matthew 26:51-52 and Mark 14:47 do not name him.
25606: The scene is often used to teach that Jesus' kingdom is not advanced by violence and that he showed mercy even to those arresting him.
25608: Many scholars think John's naming of Malchus, and of a relative of his, shows contact with someone who knew the high priest's household (compare John 18:15-16).
25609: A servant doing his master's errand who never expected to be touched by the man he came to seize; shaken and quiet.
25614: Disciple and financial supporter of Jesus
25618: Travels with Jesus and supports the mission
25619: Healed by Jesus of 'evil spirits and infirmities', she joins the women who travel with him and the Twelve and provide for them out of their own means.
25620: Goes to the tomb and reports to the apostles
25621: She is among the women who watch the burial, prepare spices, find the tomb empty, hear the angels, and tell the apostles, who at first do not believe them.
25622: Joanna was a Galilean woman whom Jesus had healed, and the wife of Chuza, the steward (household manager) of Herod Antipas. That means she came from the edge of the royal court, the same court that executed John the Baptist. She travelled with Jesus, helped pay for the mission, and was one of the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles. She appears only in Luke.
25623: Luke 8:3 calls her 'the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward' and says she and others provided for Jesus' group from their possessions. Luke 24:10 lists her with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James as those who told the apostles about the empty tomb.
25624: Luke may have known Herod's court partly through her (compare Luke 23:8-12 and Manaen in Acts 13:1); this is a suggestion, not something the text says.
25626: Richard Bauckham has argued she is the same person as Junia in Romans 16:7, using a Latin name; most scholars treat this as possible but unproven (speculative).
25627: Well-spoken and composed, with the manners of a court household, but warm and direct about what Jesus did for her.
25629: Travels with Jesus and the Twelve
25630: Named among the women healed by Jesus who travel with him and support the group from their own means.
25631: Susanna is named once, in Luke 8:3, among the women who travelled with Jesus and paid for the mission out of their own money. Nothing else is known about her. Her mention shows that Jesus' traveling company included several women of some means, not only the Twelve.
25632: Luke 8:2-3 lists her after Mary Magdalene and Joanna, as one of 'many others' who provided for them.
25633: Quiet and practical, the sort who keeps the group fed and says little about it.
25636: Possibly the mother of the sons of Zebedee
25638: Witness of the crucifixion and empty tomb
25640: She is among the women from Galilee who had followed and served Jesus and who watch his death from a distance.
25642: Early on the first day of the week she goes with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James to anoint the body, and finds the stone rolled away.
25643: Salome was a Galilean woman who followed Jesus, watched his crucifixion, and went to the tomb on Easter morning. Mark is the only Gospel that names her. She is not the same person as Salome the daughter of Herodias, who is never named in the Bible.
25644: Mark 15:40 lists her with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses. Mark 16:1 has her buy spices to anoint Jesus' body.
25646: Matthew's parallel list (Matt 27:56) has 'the mother of the sons of Zebedee' where Mark has Salome, so many readers conclude she was the mother of James and John.
25648: Some also identify her with 'his mother's sister' in John 19:25, which would make her Jesus' aunt and James and John his cousins. Others read John 19:25 differently, and the link remains uncertain.
25649: Steady and loyal, with a mother's bluntness; she stays when others run.
25651: Mary (from Hebrew Miryam); 'of Clopas' can mean wife, or less likely daughter, of Clopas
25654: Possibly Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses
25658: John names her among the women standing near the cross with Jesus' mother and Mary Magdalene.
25659: Mary the wife of Clopas is named only in John 19:25, standing by the cross. Who she was beyond that is debated. Many identify her with 'Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses' in Mark and with 'the other Mary' in Matthew, who also went to the tomb. If so, she was one of the first witnesses of the resurrection.
25660: John 19:25 lists 'his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene'. The Greek can be read as three women (with Mary of Clopas being the mother's sister) or four women.
25661: Identification with Mary mother of James and Joses (debated)
25662: The lists of women at the cross (Mark 15:40; Matt 27:56) include a Mary who is mother of James the younger and Joses; many scholars take her to be the same as Mary of Clopas. Others think these are different women.
25664: If John lists three women, she is called the 'sister' of Jesus' mother. Since two sisters are unlikely to share the name Mary, many take 'sister' loosely as sister-in-law, which fits the report that Clopas was Joseph's brother.
25665: Hegesippus, a second-century Jewish Christian writer, says Clopas was the brother of Joseph and that his son Symeon became leader of the Jerusalem church after James.
25667: A family woman, steady and grieving, who speaks of Jesus almost as kin.
25671: Disciple who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus
25673: On Easter Sunday he and a companion walk to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. A stranger joins them and explains from the Scriptures why the Messiah had to suffer. At supper he breaks bread, they recognize Jesus, and he vanishes. They hurry back to Jerusalem to tell the eleven.
25674: Leaves Jerusalem downcast on the first day of the week.
25675: Recognizes the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread.
25676: Returns the same hour to report to the eleven.
25677: Cleopas was one of two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus without recognizing him. His companion is not named. He is a follower outside the Twelve, and his story is one of the most detailed resurrection appearances in the Gospels.
25678: Luke 24:18 names him. Luke 24:21 records his disappointment: 'we had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel'. Luke 24:32 records the two saying their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures.
25680: Some identify him with Clopas, the husband of one of the Marys at the cross (John 19:25); if so, his unnamed companion may have been his wife. Others note that Kleopas (a Greek name) and Klōpas (probably Semitic) are spelled differently and may be different men.
25681: The Emmaus story is often read as a model for Christian worship: Scripture opened, then bread broken, and Jesus known in both.
25682: Honest about his disappointment, quick to talk, and then bursting with excitement.
25683: The Samaritan woman at the well
25684: The text does not give her name
25687: Witness to her town about Jesus
25691: At noon Jesus, tired, asks her for a drink. She is surprised, since Jews and Samaritans avoided sharing vessels. He speaks of 'living water', reveals that she has had five husbands and lives with a man who is not her husband, and discusses where God should be worshipped. He then tells her plainly that he is the Messiah.
25693: She leaves her water jar and tells the townspeople, 'Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.' Many believe because of her word, and more after hearing Jesus for two days.
25694:
This unnamed Samaritan woman had the longest recorded one-to-one conversation with Jesus in the Gospels. Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem; Jews and Samaritans were long-standing rivals. Jesus crossed that line, and the line between men and women in public, to speak with her. She became the first person in John's Gospel to tell a whole town about him.

Readers often assume she was an immoral outcast because she came at noon and had five husbands. The text does not say why she had five husbands; she may have been widowed or divorced (only men could initiate divorce), and many scholars now caution against reading her mainly as a 'sinful woman'.
25695: John 4:9 says Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. John 4:18 says she has had five husbands and the man she now has is not her husband. John 4:26 has Jesus say 'I who speak to you am he.' John 4:39 says many Samaritans believed because of her testimony.
25697: Many preachers present her as a woman with a scandalous past whom Jesus gently exposes and restores.
25699: Others stress that the text never calls her sinful, and that she acts like a theological conversation partner and an evangelist, much like the disciples who bring others to Jesus in John 1.
25700: She is honoured as a saint and 'equal to the apostles' for her preaching.
25701: Orthodox tradition names her Photini (or Photina, 'the enlightened one') and says she preached widely and was martyred under the emperor Nero. The text itself gives no name.
25702: Orthodox Synaxarion; commemorated on the Sunday of the Samaritan Woman, the fifth Sunday after Pascha
25703: Sharp, quick-witted and unafraid to argue theology with a stranger; then eager and breathless as she runs to tell others.
25706: Pharisee who hosted Jesus for a meal
25707: Pharisee (member of a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law)
25708: A sinful woman anoints Jesus at his table
25709: While Jesus eats at Simon's house, a woman known as a sinner weeps on his feet, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them. Simon privately doubts Jesus is a prophet. Jesus tells him a parable of two debtors and points out that Simon gave him no water, kiss or oil, while she has shown great love because she has been forgiven much.
25710: Simon was a Pharisee in Galilee who invited Jesus to dinner. When a woman with a bad reputation came in and anointed Jesus' feet, Simon judged both her and Jesus, and Jesus answered with a short parable about forgiveness. The story is told only in Luke and leaves Simon's response open.
25711: Luke 7:36 says a Pharisee invited Jesus; Luke 7:40 gives his name as Simon. Luke 7:39 records his inner thought that a prophet would know what sort of woman she was. Luke 7:44-46 lists the courtesies he did not offer.
25713: Mark, Matthew and John tell of an anointing at Bethany in Jesus' last week, Mark and Matthew at the house of 'Simon the leper'. Some think Luke's story is a different, earlier event; others think the Gospels preserve varied forms of one event. Most scholars treat Luke's account as a separate event or a separate tradition.
25715: Simon stands for the respectable person who sees others' sins more readily than his own need of forgiveness.
25716: Polite, reserved and quietly judgmental, a careful host who keeps a guest at arm's length.
25718: 'Simon the leper', probably a man once ill with a skin disease, perhaps healed
25721: Two days before Passover, while Jesus is at table in Simon's house, a woman pours very costly ointment on his head. Some complain about the waste; Jesus says she has anointed his body for burial and will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached.
25722: Simon the leper lived at Bethany near Jerusalem and hosted a meal for Jesus in the last week before his death. He is known only by this nickname. Since a person with an active skin disease would have lived apart from others, many think he had been healed, possibly by Jesus, though the text does not say so.
25723: Mark 14:3 and Matthew 26:6 place the anointing 'in the house of Simon the leper' at Bethany. John 12:1-8 tells of a dinner at Bethany where Martha served, Lazarus reclined, and Mary anointed Jesus' feet, but does not name the host.
25725: Many think John's dinner at Bethany is the same event, held at Simon's house. Some later writers guessed Simon was a relative of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, or even their father; this is speculation.
25727: A minority identify him with Simon the Pharisee of Luke 7, treating the anointings as one event; most scholars keep them apart.
25728: Grateful and hospitable, a man who knows what it is to be shut out and now opens his door.
25733: Instigator of John the Baptist's execution
25735: Leaves her husband to marry Antipas
25736: She divorces her first husband, Herod Antipas's half-brother, and marries Antipas. John the Baptist publicly condemns the marriage as against the Law (Lev 18:16).
25737: Demands the head of John the Baptist
25738: She holds a grudge against John. At Herod's birthday banquet her daughter pleases Herod with a dance and, prompted by Herodias, asks for John's head on a platter.
25740: According to Josephus, when the emperor Caligula banished Antipas to Gaul, he offered to spare Herodias, but she chose to go into exile with her husband.
25741: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great who married two of her uncles in turn. Her second marriage, to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, was publicly condemned by John the Baptist, since she had left Antipas's brother while he was still alive. The Gospels present her as the driving force behind John's beheading. The Jewish historian Josephus adds that she later went with Antipas into exile in Gaul in AD 39.
25742: Mark 6:17-18 says Herod married Herodias, 'his brother Philip's wife', and John said it was not lawful. Mark 6:19 says she nursed a grudge and wanted to kill John but could not, until the banquet. Luke 3:19 says John rebuked Herod about Herodias.
25743: Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.5.4) says she was the daughter of Aristobulus, a son of Herod the Great, and that her first husband was a son of Herod the Great called simply Herod. Mark calls this first husband Philip. Some think he had a double name; others think Mark confused him with Philip the tetrarch, who in fact married Herodias's daughter (debated). Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.7.1-2) tells of her ambition pushing Antipas to seek the title of king, which led to his downfall.
25745: She is often compared to Jezebel, the queen who hunted the prophet Elijah (1 Kgs 19:2), with John playing the role of a new Elijah.
25746: Josephus gives a political reason for John's death (Herod feared an uprising), while the Gospels give a personal one; many historians think both factors could be true together.
25747: Proud, calculating and fiercely protective of her position; speaks with cold precision.
